cards.q: A DOGS table has fields dog_name, breed, dob and microchip. Two of the six dogs are called fido. Why is dog_name a poor primary key?
cards.right: Its values are not unique
wrong: A primary key must be a number
A primary key must be the first field
It is a foreign key in another table
cards.why: A primary key must be different in every record. fido appears twice, so dog_name can't pick out one dog.
cards.hook: Primary key = one value, one record. Any repeat rules a field out.

cards.q: In the DOGS table no breed repeats among the six dogs shown. Why is breed still a poor choice of primary key?
cards.right: Two dogs could share a breed later
wrong: It is unique, so it is a good key
A String field can't be a key
Breeds are written in lower case
cards.why: A key must stay unique as records are added. Another labrador could join, so breed can't be guaranteed unique.
cards.hook: Unique today isn't enough: it must stay unique for every record added.

cards.q: One owner can own many dogs, and every dog's row repeats its owner's owner_id, name and address. How does a foreign key improve this design?
cards.right: OWNERS table; owner_id as FK in DOGS
wrong: DOGS table; dog_id as FK in OWNERS
Add dog_id to the same single table
cards.why: Split it into OWNERS (primary key owner_id) and DOGS. owner_id in DOGS is a foreign key, so each owner is stored once and linked to many dogs.
cards.hook: The foreign key goes on the "many" side: each dog points to its one owner.

cards.q: The dog table is split into OWNERS and DOGS, and owner_id is in both tables. What is owner_id in each table?
cards.right: PK in OWNERS, FK in DOGS
wrong: FK in OWNERS, PK in DOGS
cards.why: owner_id identifies one owner, so it is the primary key of OWNERS; in DOGS it refers to that owner, so it is a foreign key.
cards.hook: A foreign key is another table's primary key.

cards.q: Alex's BOOKS table has fields book_id, title, year, cost, author, author_dob and on_loan, with four books. In this table, what is a record?
cards.right: One row: all the fields about one book
cards.why: A record is a single row of related fields about one item, e.g. book 1, The Cat in the Hat. A column is a field.
cards.hook: Record = a row (across). Field = a column (down).

cards.q: Alex keeps her Dr. Seuss books in a database with a table called BOOKS. What is a database?
cards.right: An organised collection of data
wrong: The hard drive the data is saved on
A program for calculating in cells
cards.why: A database is an organised collection of structured data, kept in tables so it can be easily retrieved, added to, updated and deleted.
cards.hook: Database = organised data you can search, add, change and delete.

cards.q: BOOKS has book_id (1, 2, 3, 4), title, year (1957, 1960, 1954, 1957), cost, author (Dr. Seuss for most) and on_loan. Which field is the best primary key?
cards.right: book_id
cards.why: book_id is unique: each book gets its own number. year repeats (1957 twice), author repeats, and two books could share a title.
cards.hook: Pick the ID field: it is made to be unique.

cards.q: Alex chooses book_id as the primary key of her BOOKS table. How should she justify that choice?
cards.right: Its value is unique for each record
wrong: It is the first column in the table
Keys must be numbers, and it is one
cards.why: A primary key must identify exactly one record, so its value must be unique: book_id is guaranteed different for every book.
cards.hook: Justify a key with one word: unique.

cards.q: The cost field of BOOKS holds 6.95, 8.95, €10 and 9.95. Why is €10 a data inconsistency?
cards.right: It is written in a different format
cards.why: Inconsistent data is the same kind of fact written differently: €10 has a euro sign and no decimals, the others are plain numbers like 6.95.
cards.hook: Inconsistent = same kind of data, different format.

cards.q: The on_loan field of BOOKS holds Yes, Y, N and No for its four books. What is the inconsistency?
cards.right: Yes/Y and No/N mean the same things
wrong: Two books are on loan, two are not
cards.why: Yes and Y both mean on loan, N and No both mean not on loan: one value written in two ways, so a search for Yes misses Y.
cards.hook: Pick one spelling for each value and stick to it.
keys: one value written in two ways

cards.q: The author field of BOOKS reads Dr. Seuss, Dr. Seuss, Doc Seus, Dr. Seuss. What problem does Doc Seus cause?
cards.right: A search for Dr. Seuss misses it
wrong: It makes author a good primary key
cards.why: It is an inconsistency: the database can't tell Doc Seus means Dr. Seuss, so a query for author = 'Dr. Seuss' misses Horton Hears a Who!
cards.hook: Computers match text exactly: one wrong letter is a different value.
keys: can't tell Doc Seus means Dr. Seuss

cards.q: With its inconsistencies fixed, BOOKS has book_id (1–4), title, year (1957…), cost (6.95, 8.95, 10.00, 9.95), author, author_dob and on_loan (Yes/No). Which field is Real?
cards.right: cost
cards.why: Real is a number with a decimal part: cost (6.95, 9.95). year and book_id are whole numbers (Integer); on_loan is Boolean.
cards.hook: Real has a point: 6.95. Integer is whole: 1957.
keys: a number with a decimal part

cards.q: With its inconsistencies fixed, the on_loan field of BOOKS holds only Yes or No. Which data type is it?
cards.right: Boolean
cards.why: Boolean holds one of two values (true/false, yes/no), so on_loan, which is only ever Yes or No, is Boolean.
cards.hook: Only two possible values? Boolean.

cards.q: LOANS (member_id, book_id, date_borrowed) has a row ?, 4, 01/05/24. Amy is member 1 and borrowed book 4 (How the Grinch Stole Christmas!) on 1 May. What is the missing member_id?
cards.why: LOANS stores keys, not names: Amy's member_id in MEMBERS is 1, so the row reads 1, 4, 01/05/24.
cards.hook: A LOANS row is keys and a date: who, which book, when.

cards.q: The exam was on Wednesday 22 May 2024. Chloe borrowed Horton Hears a Who! "7 days ago". What date goes in date_borrowed?
cards.why: Count back 7 days from 22 May: 22 − 7 = 15, so the date is 15/05/2024.
cards.hook: "Ago" means count back from the day of the exam.

cards.q: Chloe is member 3 and Horton Hears a Who! is book 3. She borrowed it on 15/05/2024. Which row is added to LOANS (member_id, book_id, date_borrowed)?
cards.why: Each column takes a key: Chloe's member_id is 3 and Horton's book_id is 3, then the date: 3, 3, 15/05/2024.
cards.hook: Look each name up in its own table and write its key.

cards.q: A library has MEMBERS (member_id, member_name) and LOANS (member_id, book_id, date_borrowed). Which field of LOANS is a foreign key?
cards.right: member_id
cards.why: member_id in LOANS holds a primary key from MEMBERS, so it is a foreign key (book_id is one too, from BOOKS).
cards.hook: Spot an FK: a column that is another table's primary key.
keys: holds a primary key from MEMBERS

cards.q: In the library design, what does the foreign key member_id do in the LOANS table?
cards.right: Links each loan to its member
wrong: Stores the member's name in LOANS
Links each member to a book title
cards.why: A foreign key links two tables: member_id in LOANS holds a member's primary key, so each loan points to the member who borrowed the book.
cards.hook: Primary key: identifies. Foreign key: links.

cards.q: The library has BOOKS, MEMBERS and LOANS (member_id, book_id, date_borrowed). Why does BOOKS no longer need its on_loan field?
cards.right: A LOANS record shows the book is out
wrong: BOOKS already has a primary key
cards.why: If a book has a record in LOANS it is on loan, and its date borrowed can be looked up too, so on_loan in BOOKS would repeat that fact.
cards.hook: If another table already shows it, don't store it again.

cards.q: Relational databases reduce data redundancy. What is data redundancy?
cards.right: The same data stored in several places
wrong: Data that is no longer needed
Data stored in the wrong type
cards.why: Data redundancy is a single piece of data stored in more than one place in a database, e.g. Dr. Seuss typed into every BOOKS record.
cards.hook: Redundant = repeated. Store each fact once.

cards.q: In Alex's single BOOKS table the author and author_dob are typed into every record. Why is this data redundancy bad practice?
cards.right: The copies can become inconsistent
wrong: It makes the data harder to back up
It stops a table having a primary key
It makes queries return no rows
cards.why: Repeated copies waste storage, and when one copy changes and another doesn't they disagree, as Doc Seus and Dr. Seuss do.
cards.hook: Two copies of a fact will drift apart.

cards.q: A data analytics project starts with a hypothesis. Which is a hypothesis Alex's library data could test?
cards.right: The Cat in the Hat is borrowed most
wrong: Add a LOANS table to the database
Clean the data before analysing it
cards.why: A hypothesis is a statement that the data can show to be true or false; a question or a task is not a hypothesis.
cards.hook: A hypothesis is a statement you can test, not a question.

cards.q: Alex's hypothesis: "More books are borrowed in summer than in winter." Which LOANS field must she analyse to test it?
cards.right: date_borrowed
cards.why: The hypothesis is about the time of year, so it needs the date of every loan: date_borrowed, counted by season.
cards.hook: Match the hypothesis to the field that measures it.

cards.q: The date_borrowed field holds 20/05/2024, 01/05/24 and 18/05/2024. Which type of data error does data cleaning fix here?
cards.right: Inconsistent formatting
cards.why: One kind of data is written in two date formats; cleaning rewrites them all in one standard format, dd/mm/yyyy.
cards.hook: Same data, different look: inconsistent formatting.

cards.q: Data cleaning finds duplicate records in the LOANS table. What is usually done with them?
cards.right: Find them and remove the copies
wrong: Fill them in with an average value
Convert them to the right data type
Keep them: more data is better
cards.why: Repeated entries skew counts and statistics, so they are identified and removed, leaving each record once.
cards.hook: Duplicates: remove. Missing: fill in or remove. Formats: standardise.

cards.q: A Deposit Return Scheme app has a database management component. Which is a specific use case for it?
cards.right: Store each machine's location, status
wrong: Read the screen aloud to users
Test each component as it is written
cards.why: A database stores records: e.g. each RVM's location, date last emptied and status, or the deposits and refunds for financial reports.
cards.hook: A database use case = what records it keeps and what they're used for.

cards.q: The DRS database tracks every returned container with a unique identifier, its size, its deposit and the machine that took it. Which is the primary key?
cards.right: The container's unique identifier
cards.why: Only the identifier is different for every container: many containers share a size, a deposit (15c or 25c) or a machine.
cards.hook: The primary key is the field that is never the same twice.
